newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia oilmen start slowdown, impact unclear.
newsitem.headline: Colombia oilmen start slowdown, impact unclear.

text.p: Colombia's main oil workers' union began a slowdown Tuesday in preparation for a possible all-out strike but it was not immediately clear what impact this had on production levels.

Officials at the state-run oil company Ecopetrol in Bogota declined to say whether production or refining had been hit. A regional official, meanwhile, said pumping operations along the country's two main pipelines -- paralyzed by a 24-hour strike by the USO union in October -- were normal.

The job action by the 5,700-strong USO follows the approval of a strike motion Monday night, which union leaders said would only come into effect if talks with government ministers, which began last Sunday, collapsed.
"Production is not 100 percent. I don't have any figures but as days go by then production will drop because workers will not be working 100 percent," USO leader Hernando Hernandez said.

The strike motion was passed in the wake of the arrest of 14 men -- 11 of them USO members -- since last Thursday on charges of sabotaging oil pipelines and of links to the National Liberation Army (ELN), Colombia's second largest guerrilla force.

Further arrests may also be carried out in the next few days, a spokesman for the chief prosecutor's office said. He did not say whether the action would be taken against USO members or private individuals.
But Hernandez stressed Tuesday that the strike call was also in protest at what the union sees as the government's plans for the creeping privatization of Ecopetrol.

Ecopetrol chairman Luis Bernardo Florez was huddled in meetings with top company officials Tuesday to discuss the implications of a possible indefinite strike. A spokesman was unable to give figures on possible lost production as a result of the industrial action.

In the northern oil production center of Barrancabermeja, local USO representative Julian Parra said refining operations were being slowed but could not say what percentage of the daily average of 230,000 barrels would not be processed.
An Ecopetrol official at a pumping station near Barrancabermeja said operations along the country's two main oil pipelines, which pump about 350,000 barrels a day, were "absolutely normal."
The USO union leaders were scheduled to meet with heads of other oil industry labor organizations in a bid to spread the strike threat to the private sector, including multinationals.

The USO's influence spread beyond Ecopetrol after a merger in mid-October. The USO national directorate is due to resume talks with government ministers this week in an effort to avert the strike but no time and date has yet been announced.
